comparison: Perfect agreement on cellular-level mechanisms (C7, C26-C28). Both evaluations support the two-photon calcium imaging findings showing distinct neuronal ensembles, sequential tiling, and shifts in neuronal tuning after learning. OpenEval emphasizes mechanistic validation of bulk photometry; peer reviewers highlight the shift in temporal activity as a potential mechanism linking extended motivation to reward maximization.

Perfect agreement on literature-based contextual claims (C30-C39). Both evaluations support these background claims about PFC lesions, ACC function, OFC function, and goal-directed learning. OpenEval notes they align with current field understanding; peer reviewers accept the theoretical framework while highlighting the novelty of the current work.

Perfect agreement on methodological claims (C40-C59). Both evaluations fully support the comprehensive methodological details including equipment specifications, behavioral protocols, analysis methods, and intervention parameters. OpenEval describes them as internally consistent and reproducible; peer reviewers explicitly endorse methods as 'state-of-the-art.'

Strong agreement on OFC→ACC ramp findings (C5-C6, C22-C25). Both evaluations support the projection-specific photometry showing ramping patterns across trial sequences. OpenEval emphasizes the Learner vs Non-Learner comparison and pathway specificity; peer reviewers highlight the continuous ramping in 'fast learner' subgroup as an interesting concept for implementing extended motivational signals.

Strong agreement on ACC motivation-related signals (C1-C4, C10-C11). Both evaluations support photometry recordings, behavioral correlations, and causal manipulations showing ACC's role in learning. OpenEval includes C9 and emphasizes temporal precedence and persistence across unrewarded trials; peer reviewers include C14-C16 and describe evidence as 'compelling' and 'convincing.'

Agreement on mechanistic interpretation (C8, C29, C62, C66). Both evaluations support the optogenetic inhibition showing context-dependent impairments and the mechanistic model. OpenEval includes C60, C67-C68 and notes some aspects remain interpretive; peer reviewers describe the evidence as 'convincing' and highlight the contribution to understanding how brain areas translate motivation into action.

Agreement on causal manipulation findings (C17-C19). Both evaluations support the task-specificity and critical period requirements shown through optogenetic inhibition. OpenEval includes broader temporal dissociation and learning correlation claims (C12-C16); peer reviewers focus on the causal role findings and describe the combination of recording and inhibition experiments as 'impressive' and 'generally accepted.'

Divergent evaluation of speculative claims (C61, C64-C65). OpenEval rates these as UNCERTAIN, explicitly noting they are speculative hypotheses lacking direct experimental support. Peer reviewers rate them as SUPPORTED, accepting the interpretations without challenge and noting the findings 'will be valuable for further research,' though one reviewer suggests 'theoretical analysis seems to be incomplete.'

Both address projection-specific findings. OpenEval R3 covers broader OFC→ACC ramp claims (C5-C6, C20-C25); peer R7 specifically addresses comparative projection findings (C20-C21). Both support the projection-specific analyses, with peer reviewers noting the 'combination of investigation of ACC neurons and of OFC regions projecting to ACC are very impressive.'

Partial overlap on behavioral findings (C12-C13). OpenEval R2 covers temporal dissociation and learning correlations (C12-C19); peer R5 addresses behavioral measures (C9, C12-C13). Both support these findings, with peer reviewers noting the task is 'appropriate to identify correlates of relevant cognitive and behavioural variables.'

Partial overlap on learning correlations (C14-C16). OpenEval R2 emphasizes temporal dissociation and critical period (C12-C19); peer R1 focuses on ACC motivation signals including learning correlations (C1-C4, C10-C11, C14-C16). Both support the temporal precedence of neural activity and its correlation with learning.

Agreement on foraging analogy (C63). OpenEval R9 supports the conceptual parallel to foraging behavior as reasonable but interpretive; peer R10 accepts this interpretation along with other conceptual claims. Both evaluations support the foraging framework, though OpenEval notes it remains an interpretive framework rather than directly tested.

Partial overlap on interpretive claims (C60, C67-C68). OpenEval R5 includes mechanistic model claims (C8, C29, C60, C62, C66-C68) and rates them as SUPPORTED despite noting some aspects are interpretive; peer R10 covers broader interpretive claims (C60-C61, C63-C65, C67-C68) and accepts them as SUPPORTED, noting they provide 'a promising concept' though theoretical analysis could be more extensive.

Minimal overlap on behavioral correlation (C9). OpenEval R1 includes behavioral correlations as part of broader ACC motivation evidence (C1-C4, C9-C11); peer R5 addresses behavioral measures (C9, C12-C13) as part of task validation. Both support the behavioral findings without challenge.
